entry.title: How I Plan to Review Apps and Software
entry.summary: The framework I will use for future app and software reviews.
entry.content:
How I Plan to Review Apps and Software

I don't want my reviews to be just a list of features.

A feature can exist and still be frustrating to use.

So I plan to evaluate software from the perspective of actually using it.

What I will look at

1. First impression

Is it easy to understand what the application does?

2. Everyday usability

How does it feel after using it for several days?

3. Performance

Does it remain responsive with normal workloads?

4. Design

Is the interface clear, consistent and accessible?

5. Privacy and trust

What data does the product collect and what permissions does it request?

6. Value

Is the product worth the money or the time it asks from the user?

The most important rule

I will try to separate facts from my opinion.

That makes a review more useful and more honest.

entry.title: My Personal Website Stack: Python, Pelican and Markdown
entry.summary: Why I chose a Python static-site generator instead of building a full web application.
entry.content:
My Personal Website Stack

For a personal blog, I don't need a database, login system or a large backend.

I need a reliable way to write content and turn it into a fast website.

The stack

Markdown
   ↓
Pelican
   ↓
Jinja2
   ↓
HTML + CSS
   ↓
GitHub Pages

Python sits at the center because Pelican is Python-based.

Why static?

A static website is easy to host, easy to version-control and difficult to accidentally break with a database problem.

Every article is just a Markdown file.

That makes the content portable and transparent.

Why not Django?

Django is excellent, but it solves a much bigger problem.

If I eventually need accounts, dynamic data, an API or user-generated content, a backend may make sense.

For a personal blog, it would mostly be extra machinery.

The learning value

The best part is that the site itself becomes a CSE project.

I get to practice:

  • Python
  • templating
  • HTML/CSS
  • Git
  • CI/CD
  • web accessibility
  • SEO
  • static-site architecture

And I get a website at the end.

That's a good trade.

entry.title: Why I Started Building My Own Website
entry.summary: Why I wanted a personal space for writing, experiments, reviews and everything that doesn't belong in a portfolio.
entry.content:
Why I Started Building My Own Website

A portfolio is useful, but it only tells part of the story.

It shows projects, skills and achievements. It doesn't really show the small experiments, strange bugs, useful tools, personal discoveries or lessons that happen between those polished results.

So I wanted another place.

What I want to write about

This site will be a mixture of:

  • technical notes
  • programming experiments
  • robotics projects
  • AI and ML findings
  • software and app reviews
  • interesting tools and websites
  • university experiences
  • life updates and personal thoughts

Not every post will be deeply technical. Some will simply be something I found useful and want to remember.

Why Pelican?

I wanted the site itself to be a learning project.

Pelican gives me a Python-based static-site workflow while still letting me work directly with HTML, CSS, Jinja2 and Markdown.

That means the website can stay simple while I learn from the system behind it.

The goal

I don't want this to be a website that looks finished and then never changes.

I want it to become a record of learning and building.

Let's see where it goes.

entry.title: Building an Indoor Food Delivery Robot
entry.summary: A development log for my indoor food delivery robot project.
entry.content:
Building an Indoor Food Delivery Robot

One of my current project interests is an indoor food delivery robot.

The basic idea is simple: a small mobile robot should carry food from one point to another inside a controlled environment.

The engineering challenge is making the simple idea reliable.

What I am exploring

The project involves several areas:

  • motor control
  • obstacle detection
  • line detection
  • sensor integration
  • embedded programming
  • navigation logic
  • power management
  • physical design

Why this is interesting

A robot that moves from point A to point B sounds easy until the real world gets involved.

A sensor gives noisy readings. Motors don't behave identically. The robot can drift away from a line. An obstacle can appear unexpectedly.

Those problems make the project much more valuable as a learning experience.

Current direction

I'm experimenting with ESP32-based control and different sensor arrangements.

Future posts will document the circuit, control logic, testing results and the mistakes that happen along the way.

This page is intentionally a development log rather than a polished final report.
